subject: physics
title: Junction Run
summary: Bias a p–n junction to the barrier you need, match a rectifier’s output frequency and read a diode’s resistance off its V–I curve.

chapter.name: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits

concepts: The p–n junction and its barrier
learningOutcome: The student can bias a junction to a given barrier, give the output frequency of half-wave and full-wave rectifiers, and find a diode’s forward and reverse resistance from its V–I curve.

levels.title: Hopper’s barrier
levels.adds: Baseline: forward bias lowers the junction’s barrier V₀ by the battery voltage, reverse bias raises it by the same amount (Ex 14.4, 14.5; Example 14.3).
hints: Forward bias: barrier = V₀ − V. Reverse bias: barrier = V₀ + V.
If the target is lower than V₀ you need forward bias; if it is higher, reverse.

levels.title: Beat’s rhythm
levels.adds: New idea: a half-wave rectifier gives one pulse per supply cycle, a full-wave rectifier gives two, so the output is twice the supply frequency (Ex 14.6).
hints: Count how many half-cycles the diodes let through in one full cycle.
One diode: one pulse per cycle. Two diodes: one pulse per half-cycle.
The period of the supply is 1/f.

levels.title: Slope’s resistance
levels.adds: Apply it: the forward resistance is the slope ΔV/ΔI between two points on the curve, and the reverse resistance is V/I at the point (Example 14.4).
hints: Forward bias: divide the change in voltage by the change in current, in amps.
Reverse bias: divide the voltage by the current, with µA = 10⁻⁶ A.
The dial is a power of ten: 10 Ω is 1.0 and 10⁷ Ω is 7.0.

misconceptions: A diode obeys Ohm’s law with one fixed resistance
A full-wave rectifier gives the same frequency as the supply
